publication.title: The rate of return to the HighScope Perry Preschool Program

context.location: Perry Elementary School, Ypsilanti, Michigan, United States
context.population: Disadvantaged African-American children in the historical Perry study
context.period: early to mid-1960s; five entering cohorts
context.delivery: 2.5-hour preschool sessions on school weekdays and weekly teacher home visits
context.design: random assignment with subsequent reassignment; economic analysis adjusts for compromised randomization
context.sampleSizeMeaning: original assignment groups, not a verified complete-case denominator for every outcome
context.earningsImputation: kernel matching using NLSY for missing earnings before age 40
context.uncertaintyMethod: Monte Carlo resampling of prediction errors and bootstrapping; Table 1 notes and Appendix K
context.uncertaintyLimit: standard errors cover estimable model components; other assumptions are examined through sensitivity analysis

cost.denominator: per child for the preschool program
cost.scope: initial program resource cost: operating expenses, including teachers and administration, plus classrooms and facilities
cost.basis: reported estimate from Barnett (1996), as used by Heckman et al. (2010)
cost.warning: Not annual expenditure and not the financing-adjusted denominator under every deadweight-loss scenario

notes: IRRs are annual real rates expressed as percent in the source; convert both estimate and SE to fractions if using fractional-rate properties.
Benefit/cost ratios and their SEs are dimensionless ratios, not percentages or annual returns.
The varying first-column label is deadweight loss for IRR rows but discount rate for benefit/cost rows.
Deadweight loss is welfare loss per tax dollar; all benefit/cost rows assume 50% deadweight loss.
High murder valuation is $4.1 million and includes a statistical value of life; low valuation is $13,000 and excludes that component.
Society includes participants and the general public.
All is computed from pooled average profiles; it is not the arithmetic average of male and female IRRs.
Nine crime categories are included; missing components and extrapolation prevent interpretation as wholly observed cash flows.
Individual benefit/cost cells are dashes in this table, not zero estimates.

table2SelectedObservedOutcomes.kind: descriptive group means and standard errors; not adjusted causal contrasts
